headline: Bank of England raises Bank Rate to 4% in first increase since August 2023

terms.meaning: The main interest rate set by the Bank of England, which influences what banks charge and pay.
The nine-member group at the Bank that votes on interest rates.
A narrow sea route in the Gulf through which much of the world's oil passes.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises Bank Rate to 4% in first increase since August 2023
levels.body:
The Bank of England raised Bank Rate by 0.25 percentage points, from 3.75% to 4%, on Thursday 5 November. It is the first rise in more than three years.
The Monetary Policy Committee voted 8 to 1. The single dissenter wanted a larger rise of 0.5 points, to 4.25%. The Bank expects inflation to climb to about 5% by the middle of 2027, up from 3.5% in the 12 months to September, when motor fuel prices were the main driver.
The Bank blames the rise in energy costs on the war with Iran, which began when the United States and Israel attacked on 28 February, and on bottlenecks in the Strait of Hormuz. Governor Andrew Bailey said the increase should not be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes, but added that, unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, it does not seem likely to be the last. The next decision is due on 17 December.
levels.why: Higher borrowing costs affect mortgages, loans and savings, and the Bank says inflation could rise much further.

levels.headline: Bank of England lifts interest rate to 4%, the first rise in over three years
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised its main interest rate, Bank Rate, from 3.75% to 4%. It is the first increase since August 2023.
Eight members of the Monetary Policy Committee backed the quarter-point rise. One wanted a bigger move, to 4.25%. The Bank now expects inflation to reach about 5% by mid-2027. In September it stood at 3.5%, pushed up mainly by the price of petrol and diesel.
Officials link the problem to the Iran war and disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, which has pushed up energy prices. Governor Andrew Bailey said this should not be seen as the start of a long run of rises, but that more increases look likely unless the conflict in the Middle East ends. The Bank's next rate decision is scheduled for 17 December.
levels.why: The decision changes borrowing costs for households and firms and signals how worried the Bank is about prices.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises interest rates to 4% to fight rising inflation
levels.body:
The Bank of England has increased interest rates for the first time in more than three years. Bank Rate rose by a quarter of a percentage point, from 3.75% to 4%.
The committee that sets the rate voted 8 to 1 for the rise. One member wanted a larger increase. The Bank expects inflation, the rate at which prices rise, to reach about 5% by the middle of 2027. It was 3.5% in September, largely because of higher fuel costs.
Policymakers say the war involving Iran is behind much of the pressure, because it has disrupted oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. Governor Andrew Bailey said the rise was not the start of a long series of increases, but that further rises seem likely if the conflict continues. The next decision comes on 17 December.
levels.why: Interest rates shape what people pay on mortgages and loans and what they earn on savings.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises interest rates to 4%
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4%. It is the first rise since August 2023.
Eight of the nine members of the Bank's rate-setting committee voted for the increase. The other wanted a bigger rise, to 4.25%. The Bank expects inflation to hit about 5% by the middle of 2027. In September, prices were rising at 3.5% a year, driven mostly by the cost of fuel for vehicles.
The Bank says higher energy prices caused by the war with Iran, and problems shipping oil through the Strait of Hormuz, are pushing prices up. Governor Andrew Bailey said the rise should not be seen as the first of a long sequence, but did not expect it to be the last unless the Middle East conflict is settled. The next decision is on 17 December.
levels.why: It affects the cost of borrowing for homeowners, businesses and the government.

levels.headline: Bank of England puts up interest rates to 4% as prices keep climbing
levels.body:
The Bank of England has put up its main interest rate, known as Bank Rate, from 3.75% to 4%. This is the first rise in over three years. Higher rates make borrowing more expensive and are meant to slow price rises.
Eight members of the committee voted yes and one wanted an even bigger rise. The Bank thinks inflation, which is how fast prices go up, will reach about 5% by the middle of next year. In September it was 3.5%, mostly because petrol and diesel cost more.
The Bank says the war with Iran is raising energy costs, partly because oil ships are struggling to pass through the Strait of Hormuz. Governor Andrew Bailey said more rises are likely if the conflict goes on, though this is not the start of a long run. The next decision is on 17 December.
levels.why: Rates affect mortgages, loans and savings, so changes can touch most households.

levels.headline: The Bank of England raises interest rates to 4%
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised interest rates. The main rate went from 3.75% to 4%. This is the first rise for more than three years. Interest is the extra money you pay when you borrow, or earn when you save.
Banks follow this rate. So higher rates usually mean dearer mortgages and loans, and better pay on savings. The Bank hopes it will slow rising prices. Prices went up by 3.5% in the year to September, mostly because fuel cost more. The Bank thinks the figure may reach about 5% by the middle of 2027.
The Bank says the war with Iran has pushed up energy prices. The head of the Bank, Andrew Bailey, said more rises could follow if the war goes on. The next decision is on 17 December.
levels.why: Rates change what families pay on loans and mortgages and what they earn on savings.

levels.headline: Bank of England puts interest rates up to 4%
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised interest rates. It went from 3.75% to 4%. The Bank has not done this for over three years.
An interest rate is the price of borrowing money. When it goes up, loans and mortgages usually cost more. Saving can pay a little more too. The Bank wants to stop prices rising too fast. Prices rose 3.5% in the year to September, mainly because petrol and diesel got dearer. The Bank thinks it could reach about 5% by the middle of next year.
Oil and gas cost more because of the war with Iran. Ships also find it hard to use a key sea route called the Strait of Hormuz. The Bank's boss, Andrew Bailey, said more rises may come if the war goes on. The next decision is on 17 December.
levels.why: Many families will pay more on loans and mortgages, but savers may earn more.

levels.headline: Bank of England makes borrowing a bit dearer
levels.body:
The Bank of England has put up interest rates. They were 3.75% and are now 4%. Interest is the extra money you pay back when you borrow. Mortgages and loans can now cost more.
Prices have been rising fast. This is called inflation. Last year, a pound could buy more than it can now. Petrol and diesel cost more, which pushed prices up by 3.5% in a year. The Bank thinks prices could rise by about 5% by the middle of next year. Raising rates is its way of slowing that down.
There is a war with Iran. It has made oil and gas more expensive. The Bank's boss said more rises could come if the war does not end. The Bank will meet again on 17 December.
levels.why: Your family may pay more on loans, and prices may keep rising for a while.

levels.headline: The Bank of England makes borrowing cost more
levels.body:
There is a bank for the whole country. It is called the Bank of England. It has made it cost more to borrow money. Before, you paid back 3.75 extra for every 100 you borrowed in a year. Now it is 4.
Why? Prices are going up too fast. Things in shops cost more than before. Petrol costs more, too. The Bank wants to slow this down. When borrowing costs more, people spend a bit less. Then prices rise more slowly.
A war far away is part of the problem. It makes oil and gas cost more. The Bank's boss said it may do this again if the war goes on. The Bank will meet again in December.
levels.why: It could make loans and mortgages cost more for grown-ups at home.

levels.headline: A bank makes it cost more to borrow money
levels.body:
Imagine you borrow 10 pounds from a friend for a week. You give back 10 pounds and a little extra as a thank you. That little extra is called interest.
The Bank of England is like the head teacher of all the banks. It sets how much extra people pay when they borrow. This week it said the extra should be a bit bigger. Shop prices have been going up, like sweets costing more pocket money than before. Making borrowing cost more helps prices stop growing so fast.
Prices are going up because oil and gas cost more. That is because of a war far away. The Bank says it may need to do this again if the war carries on.
levels.why: It is a way of stopping prices from rising too fast, so your pocket money can buy more.

headline: S&P 500 closes up 0.31% at 7,376.86 on Friday as Nasdaq rebounds from steep sell-off

terms.meaning: An index of 500 large US companies, used as a guide to the whole stock market.
A fall of 10% or more from a recent peak.
An index dominated by technology companies.

levels.headline: S&P 500 closes up 0.31% at 7,376.86 on Friday as Nasdaq rebounds from steep sell-off
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed higher on Friday 6 November, the last completed trading session, gaining 0.31% to finish at 7,376.86. The Nasdaq Composite rose 1.09% to 24,579.42, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.46%, or 237.33 points, to 51,285.73.
The rebound followed a severe sell-off on Thursday, when the S&P 500 fell 4.36% to 7,353.73, the Nasdaq dropped 5.52% to 24,315.00 and the Dow lost 3.44%. The Nasdaq entered correction territory, meaning a fall of more than 10% from its recent record, and the so-called Magnificent Seven group of big tech firms lost about $1 trillion in value.
Investors had feared that the Democratic sweep in the midterm elections would slow the building of data centres for artificial intelligence. Chipmakers recovered on Friday, and technology was the strongest sector. Analysts disagree on whether more turbulence lies ahead.
levels.why: Share prices affect pensions and savings, and a tech sell-off can signal how nervous investors are.

levels.headline: US stocks edge higher on Friday after Thursday's sharp tech sell-off
levels.body:
The S&P 500 ended Friday 6 November up 0.31% at 7,376.86, according to CNBC. The Nasdaq Composite gained 1.09% to 24,579.42, but the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.46% to 51,285.73. Friday was the last completed session.
It was a calmer day after Thursday's rout, when the S&P 500 lost 4.36%, the Nasdaq fell 5.52% into correction territory and the Dow dropped 3.44%. About $1 trillion was wiped off the value of the Magnificent Seven tech giants, with chipmaker Nvidia hit hardest.
Investors worried that Democratic wins in the midterms could slow data-centre building, which AI firms depend on. On Friday chipmakers bounced back and information technology led the market. Some analysts expect more turbulence in the days ahead, while others see it as a reset of high valuations.
levels.why: The AI boom has driven much of the market, so a wobble matters to savers with pensions invested in shares.

levels.headline: Wall Street rebounds a little after a big tech sell-off
levels.body:
US shares ended Friday 6 November mostly higher. The S&P 500, which tracks 500 big American companies, rose 0.31% to 7,376.86. The Nasdaq, packed with tech firms, gained 1.09% to 24,579.42. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.46% to 51,285.73.
The day followed a very bad Thursday. The S&P 500 dropped 4.36%, the Nasdaq fell 5.52% and the Dow lost 3.44%. The Nasdaq is now in what traders call a correction, a drop of more than 10% from its high. The biggest tech firms lost about $1 trillion in value between them.
Investors are worried that Democratic election wins could slow the building of data centres for artificial intelligence. On Friday, chipmakers recovered some ground. Experts are split on whether the sell-off is over.
levels.why: Falling share prices can hit pension pots and make firms more cautious about spending.

levels.headline: US stocks bounce back slightly after a big fall
levels.body:
On Friday 6 November, the last full day of trading, US shares rose a little. The S&P 500, an index of 500 big companies, gained 0.31% to close at 7,376.86. The tech-heavy Nasdaq rose 1.09% to 24,579.42. The Dow Jones, which tracks 30 large firms, fell 0.46% to 51,285.73.
This came after a sharp drop on Thursday. The S&P 500 fell 4.36%, the Nasdaq fell 5.52% and the Dow fell 3.44%. The Nasdaq is now more than 10% below its peak, which traders call a correction. Big tech firms lost around $1 trillion in value.
Investors fear that the Democrats' election wins could slow the building of data centres used for artificial intelligence. Computer chip firms recovered on Friday. Some experts expect more ups and downs this week.
levels.why: Pensions and savings are often invested in shares, so big falls can matter to ordinary people.

levels.headline: US shares recover a little after a scary day
levels.body:
US shares went up a little on Friday 6 November. An index called the S&P 500, which follows 500 big firms, rose 0.31%. It closed at 7,376.86. The Nasdaq, full of tech firms, rose 1.09%. The Dow, which follows 30 big firms, fell 0.46%.
Thursday was much worse. The S&P 500 fell 4.36% and the Nasdaq fell 5.52%. That is a big drop in one day. Together, the largest tech companies lost about $1 trillion in value. A fall of more than 10% from the top is called a correction, and the Nasdaq is now in one.
Investors worry that new political changes could slow down the building of big computer centres for AI. On Friday chip makers bounced back. Nobody knows what will happen next week.
levels.why: Many pensions are invested in shares, so big swings can affect people's savings.

levels.headline: American shares rise a little after a big fall
levels.body:
Shares are small parts of companies that people can buy and sell. On Friday 6 November, American shares mostly went up a little. The S&P 500 index, which follows 500 big firms, rose 0.31%. The Nasdaq, which has lots of tech firms, rose 1.09%. The Dow, which follows 30 firms, fell 0.46%.
The day before was much worse. Prices fell 4.36% for the S&P 500 and 5.52% for the Nasdaq. Big tech firms like Nvidia lost a lot of value. People were worried that new election results might slow down AI computer centres.
On Friday, chip makers got some of their value back. Experts are not sure if prices will keep falling. Many pensions are invested in shares, so this matters to ordinary people.
levels.why: It shows how worried investors are, and it can affect pensions and jobs.

levels.headline: US shares rise a little after a big drop
levels.body:
Shares are small parts of companies. People buy and sell them every day. On Friday 6 November, the price of shares in big American companies went up a little. The main list of 500 big firms rose 0.31%. The list full of tech firms rose 1.09%. A list of 30 older, large firms fell 0.46%.
Thursday had been much worse. Prices dropped 4.36% on the main list and 5.52% on the tech list. A fall of more than 10% from the top is called a correction, and the tech list is in one. The biggest tech firms lost about a trillion dollars in value between them.
People worry that new political changes could slow the building of computer centres for AI. Chip makers bounced back on Friday. No one is sure what happens next.
levels.why: Falling prices can make people nervous about their pensions and savings.

levels.headline: Share prices wobble, then rise a little
levels.body:
Shares are tiny pieces of a company. People buy them hoping the company does well. When many people sell at once, prices fall. That happened on Thursday in America. Prices of tech companies dropped fast.
On Friday, prices rose a little. One list of 500 big companies went up 0.31%. A list full of tech companies went up 1.09%. A list of 30 old, big companies went down 0.46%. Tech firms lost about a trillion dollars in value on Thursday. That is a number too big to picture.
Some people were worried about computer centres that run AI. They thought new election results could slow them down. Experts disagree about what happens next.
levels.why: Falling prices can make people and firms nervous about spending.

levels.headline: The share market had a bad day, then a better day
levels.body:
A share market is like a giant swap shop for tiny pieces of companies. This week, lots of people wanted to sell shares in big computer companies. When many people sell, prices fall.
On Thursday, prices fell a lot. On Friday, they went up a little. It is like losing five stickers one day and getting one back the next. The main list of 500 big firms went up by a small amount. The list of tech firms went up a bit more.
Some people worried because of new election results in America. They thought it might slow down building big computer centres. Grown-ups are watching to see what happens.
levels.why: Grown-ups save money in shares, so they care when prices go up and down.

levels.headline: Prices at the big shares market went down, then up
levels.body:
Imagine a huge toy swap at school. This week lots of children wanted to swap their toys for coins at once. When that happens, toys are worth less.
That is a bit like what happened to some big companies. On Thursday their shares lost lots of value. On Friday they won a little back. It was like finding a few coins in your pocket after losing some in the playground.
Grown-ups are not sure what will happen next. They are worried about computer centres, which help machines learn. They will keep watching to see if the prices settle down.
levels.why: Many families keep savings in shares, so grown-ups pay attention when prices change.

headline: Government unveils 'earned settlement' with 10-year wait for most workers seeking to stay permanently

terms.meaning: Permission to live in the UK permanently, without time limits.
A system where people must meet conditions over time to gain permanent status.
A way of crossing the Channel without permission, often in inflatable boats.

levels.headline: Government unveils 'earned settlement' with 10-year wait for most workers seeking to stay permanently
levels.body:
The government has set out tougher rules for migrants seeking to settle in the UK. The qualifying period for indefinite leave to remain would rise from five years to 10 for most workers, under plans announced by Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood. The rules are reportedly due to take effect next year.
The highest earners could settle within three years. People earning more than £50,271, and some public service workers such as doctors, nurses and teachers, could settle after five. Care workers earning £25,000 are exempt and keep the five-year route, after pushback from unions and some Labour figures. Anyone who breached immigration rules must wait at least 20 years, and those who arrived by small boat or other clandestine means face an extra 10 years, up to 30. All applicants must meet four conditions, including a clean criminal record and high-standard English.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the previous government lost control of immigration after Brexit. Settled status will not be removed from anyone who already holds it. The government estimates more than 500,000 people will wait longer than five years. Reform UK has pledged to scrap indefinite leave to remain.
levels.why: The changes affect how long hundreds of thousands of workers must wait for security, and they are a central political issue.

levels.headline: UK sets out tougher settlement rules, doubling the usual wait to 10 years
levels.body:
The government has announced stricter rules for migrants who want to settle permanently in the UK. For most workers, the wait for indefinite leave to remain would double from five years to 10. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood announced the plan, and it is reportedly due to start next year.
Top earners could qualify after three years. Those on more than £50,271, plus some public service workers such as doctors, nurses and teachers, could qualify after five. Care workers on £25,000 are exempt after objections from unions and some Labour MPs. People who broke immigration rules wait at least 20 years, with an extra 10 for small-boat arrivals. Everyone must meet four conditions, including a clean criminal record and good English.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said numbers rose sharply after Brexit under the previous government and that Ms Mahmood has his full support. Existing settled status stays. The government says over 500,000 people will wait longer than five years. Reform UK wants to scrap the system.
levels.why: The rules decide how long migrants who work in the UK must wait for long-term security.

levels.headline: UK to make most migrants wait 10 years to settle permanently
levels.body:
The UK government has announced tougher rules for people who want to settle in Britain for good. Most workers would have to wait 10 years for indefinite leave to remain, instead of five. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood announced the plan, which is reportedly due to start next year.
There are shorter routes. The highest earners could settle after three years. People earning over £50,271, and some public service workers such as doctors, nurses and teachers, would wait five. Care workers on £25,000 keep the five-year route after complaints from unions and some Labour politicians. Those who broke immigration rules face at least 20 years, and those who arrived by small boat face 10 more. All applicants need a clean criminal record and good English.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK lost control of immigration after Brexit. People who already have settled status will keep it. Ministers expect more than 500,000 people to wait longer.
levels.why: It changes the path to permanent life in the UK for workers, and immigration is a key political divide.

levels.headline: Most migrants will wait 10 years to settle in the UK under new rules
levels.body:
The government wants most migrants who work in the UK to wait 10 years before they can settle permanently. Today the wait is usually five years. The Home Secretary, Shabana Mahmood, announced the plan, and it is reportedly meant to start next year.
Some people would wait less. The highest earners could settle after three years. People earning more than £50,271, and some public service workers such as doctors, nurses and teachers, would wait five. Care workers on £25,000 keep the five-year route, after unions and some Labour politicians complained. People who broke the rules would wait at least 20 years, and those who came by small boat would wait 10 years longer. Everyone must have no criminal record and speak good English.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the country lost control of immigration after Brexit. No one who is already settled will lose that status.
levels.why: The rules affect workers, families and employers, and immigration is a major topic in politics.

levels.headline: The UK plans a longer wait for migrants who want to stay for good
levels.body:
The UK government has announced new rules for people from other countries who want to live in Britain permanently. At the moment, most workers can apply after five years. Under the plan, they would have to wait 10 years. It is reportedly due to start next year.
Some people would wait less. Very high earners could apply after three years. People who earn more than £50,271, and some public service workers like doctors, nurses and teachers, would wait five. Care workers who earn £25,000 would also keep the five-year wait. People who broke the rules would wait at least 20 years. People who came by small boat would wait 10 years longer.
Everyone must also have no crime record and speak good English. The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, said the country lost control of immigration after Brexit. People who are already settled will not lose their status.
levels.why: It decides how long people who work here must wait to feel secure about staying.

levels.headline: Longer wait to stay in the UK for good
levels.body:
The government wants to change the rules for people from other countries who live and work in the UK. Right now, most can ask to stay for ever after five years. The plan is to make them wait 10 years instead. It may start next year.
Some people would wait less. People who earn a lot could ask after three years. Doctors, nurses and teachers could ask after five, and so could care workers. People who broke the rules would wait much longer. Those who came on small boats would wait longer still.
Everyone would also need good English and no crime record. The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, says the country lost control of immigration after Brexit. People who are already allowed to stay for ever will keep that right.
levels.why: It affects families who want to feel safe and settled in their new home.

levels.headline: New rules make it harder to settle in the UK
levels.body:
The UK has new plans for people from other countries who want to stay for good. Right now, most workers can ask after five years. The government wants them to wait 10 years instead. The plan may start next year.
Some people would wait less. People who earn a lot could ask after three years. Doctors, nurses and teachers could ask after five. So could care workers. People who broke the rules would wait much longer, at least 20 years. People who came across the sea in small boats would wait even longer.
Everyone would also need no crime record and good English. The Prime Minister said the country had lost control of its borders after Brexit. Brexit means the UK left the European Union. People who already have the right to stay will keep it.
levels.why: It affects thousands of families who live and work here and want to stay.

levels.headline: The UK wants people to wait longer before they can stay for good
levels.body:
Some people move to the UK from other countries to work. After a time, they can ask to stay for ever. Now the government wants to make them wait longer. Most would wait 10 years, not five.
Some people would wait less. People who earn a lot of money could ask sooner. So could doctors, nurses and teachers. People who broke the rules would wait much longer. People who came on small boats would wait even longer than that.
Everyone would also need to speak good English and have no crime record. The leader of the government, Prime Minister Andy Burnham, says the country lost control of its borders. People who can already stay for ever will keep that right. Not everyone agrees with the plan.
levels.why: It could change the lives of many families, and people have strong views about it.

levels.headline: Moving to a new country and staying for good
levels.body:
Imagine you move to a new school. You are allowed to stay, but only for a while. After a few years, you can ask to stay for ever. The UK has a rule like this for grown-ups who move here to work.
Until now, they could ask after five years. The government wants them to wait 10 years instead. Some people, like doctors and nurses, would not wait as long. People who broke the rules would have to wait much longer.
Everyone must also learn English well and not have broken the law. Some people think this is fair. Others think it is too hard on people who help the country. Leaders are still talking about it.
levels.why: It changes how long people who work here must wait before they feel they truly belong.

levels.headline: A new rule about staying in the country
levels.body:
Think about joining a club. At first you are a visitor. After some time, you can become a full member. In the UK, grown-ups who come from other countries can become full members too, after a wait.
The wait used to be five years. The leaders now want it to be longer, ten years. It is like the club changing the rule so you must wait twice as long. Some people, like nurses and teachers, would still wait less.
The leaders say they want the rules to be fair and clear. Some people agree. Others say it is too tough on people who work hard. Grown-ups will keep talking about it.
levels.why: It matters to families who want to feel safe and welcome in their new home.

headline: Autumn Budget temporarily doubles bank tax surcharge to 6% as borrowing forecasts rise

terms.meaning: An extra tax charged on top of the normal rate.
The Office for Budget Responsibility, the official forecaster of the public finances.
Limits the government sets itself on borrowing and debt.

levels.headline: Autumn Budget temporarily doubles bank tax surcharge to 6% as borrowing forecasts rise
levels.body:
The Autumn Budget, delivered on 28 October 2026, temporarily raises the Bank Corporation Tax Surcharge from 3% to 6%. The higher rate applies for 15 months, from 1 January 2027 to 31 March 2028, and returns to 3% from 1 April 2028.
The Treasury says the measure raises £1.5 billion to help fund support for households and businesses, while the Office for Budget Responsibility estimates it adds £1 billion to receipts in 2027-28. The OBR's forecast has borrowing at 4.2% of GDP, or £133 billion, this year. Compared with its March forecast, borrowing is higher in every year, by around £18 billion this year, mainly because of higher debt interest costs.
Economic Secretary Lucy Rigby defended the tax, saying it would ease pressure on households amid global volatility. JPMorgan boss Jamie Dimon had lobbied against higher bank taxes, but shares in London-listed lenders rose after the announcement because the increase was smaller than some had feared. The government says the measures are fully funded and meet its fiscal rules.
levels.why: Tax decisions shape support for households and show how much pressure higher borrowing costs put on the public finances.

levels.headline: Budget doubles the bank surcharge for 15 months as borrowing forecast rises
levels.body:
The Budget presented on 28 October raises the tax surcharge on banks from 3% to 6%, but only temporarily. It runs from 1 January 2027 to 31 March 2028 and falls back to 3% on 1 April 2028.
The Treasury expects £1.5 billion to help pay for support for households and businesses. The independent Office for Budget Responsibility puts the gain at £1 billion in 2027-28. It forecasts borrowing of £133 billion, or 4.2% of GDP, this year, about £18 billion more than it predicted in March, mostly because of higher interest on government debt.
Treasury minister Lucy Rigby defended the tax, saying it would help ease pressure on households. Banks had lobbied hard, including JPMorgan's Jamie Dimon, yet shares in London-listed lenders rose because the rise was smaller than feared. Ministers say the plans are fully funded and meet the fiscal rules.
levels.why: It shows how the government is paying for support while borrowing costs rise.

levels.headline: Budget raises tax on banks for 15 months to help fund support for households
levels.body:
The government's Budget on 28 October raises an extra tax on banks. The surcharge goes from 3% to 6% for 15 months, from January 2027 to March 2028. After that it falls back to 3%.
The Treasury says the change raises £1.5 billion to pay for help for households and businesses. The official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility, says the figure is closer to £1 billion in 2027-28. It also expects the government to borrow £133 billion this year, about £18 billion more than it forecast in March, mainly because interest on government debt costs more.
Treasury minister Lucy Rigby said the tax would ease pressure on households. Bank bosses had argued against it, but bank shares rose because the rise was smaller than some feared. The government says its plans are paid for and follow its own borrowing rules.
levels.why: It affects who pays for government support, and how much the state must borrow.

levels.headline: Banks to pay a higher extra tax for 15 months under the Budget
levels.body:
The Budget on 28 October puts up an extra tax on banks. The surcharge goes from 3% to 6%, but only from January 2027 to March 2028. Then it drops back to 3%.
The Treasury says it will bring in £1.5 billion to help pay for support for families and businesses. The Office for Budget Responsibility, the official forecaster, thinks the extra is about £1 billion in 2027-28. It says the government will borrow about £133 billion this year, roughly £18 billion more than it thought in March. The main reason is that interest on the national debt now costs more.
A Treasury minister, Lucy Rigby, said the tax would ease pressure on households. Banks had lobbied against it, but their share prices went up because the rise was smaller than expected. The government says its plans are fully paid for.
levels.why: It shows how the government raises money and how the cost of its debt is growing.

levels.headline: The Budget makes banks pay more tax for a while
levels.body:
The Budget is the government's yearly plan for taxes and spending. This year's, on 28 October, makes banks pay more tax for a short time. The extra tax on banks doubles from 3% to 6%. It lasts from January 2027 until March 2028. After that it goes back to 3%.
The government says this will raise about £1.5 billion to help families and businesses. An independent group that checks the numbers, called the Office for Budget Responsibility, thinks it will raise about £1 billion. It also thinks the government will borrow £133 billion this year. That is £18 billion more than it guessed in March, mostly because interest on old debts costs more.
A minister said the tax would ease pressure on households. Banks did not want it, but their share prices rose because it could have been worse.
levels.why: It helps pay for support at home and shows that the government's debts cost more than before.

levels.headline: Banks will pay a bigger tax for a short time
levels.body:
Every year the government says how it will raise and spend money. This is called the Budget. This year it said banks must pay a bigger extra tax. The extra tax goes from 3 pence in every pound of profit to 6 pence. It will last for 15 months, then fall back.
The government says this will bring in about £1.5 billion. It wants to use it to help families and businesses. A group of experts checks the government's sums. They think the government will borrow £133 billion this year. That is £18 billion more than they thought in March. Interest on old debts has become more expensive.
A minister said the tax would help families with their costs. The banks were not happy, but their share prices went up.
levels.why: The money helps pay for support at home, but the government is also borrowing more.

levels.headline: The government asks banks to pay more tax
levels.body:
The government has a plan for money every year. It is called the Budget. This time, it asked banks to pay more tax for a short while. Banks make big profits. The government will take twice as much of a special extra tax from them.
This will last for 15 months. After that, it goes back to normal. The government says it will raise about £1.5 billion. It plans to use the money to help families and firms. It also has to borrow money, and the interest on its old loans costs more now.
A minister said the extra tax would help families through hard times. Banks had asked the government not to do it.
levels.why: It shows how the country raises money to help families.

levels.headline: Banks are asked to share a little more
levels.body:
A country is a bit like a very big family with one big pot of money. The pot is filled by taxes. Every year the government decides how to fill it and how to spend it. It calls the plan the Budget.
This year the government asked banks to put more into the pot for a short time. Banks earn lots of money, so the government thinks they can share a bit more. The money will help families and businesses who are finding things hard.
The government also borrows money, like taking a loan. Interest on loans costs more than before. Banks did not want to pay more. Even so, the government decided it was fair.
levels.why: It helps the country pay for things that families need.

levels.headline: Sharing out the class tuck shop money
levels.body:
Imagine a class has a tuck shop. Every year the teacher decides how to use the tuck shop money. The teacher also decides who should add a bit more. This is a bit like what the government does with the Budget.
This time, the government asked banks to add more for a while. Banks earn lots of money, like the tuck shop selling lots of crisps. The extra money will help families and businesses who are finding life expensive.
The government also borrows money, and paying back the extra costs more than it used to. Some people think the banks should pay more, and some do not. The government has made its choice.
levels.why: It is a way of paying for help that families may need.

levels.headline: Everyone chips in to a big pot
levels.body:
A country has a very big pot of money. It pays for schools, hospitals and roads. People and companies put money in by paying tax. The government decides how much each should give. This plan is called the Budget.
This year, banks must give more for a short time. Banks earn lots of money from looking after savings and lending. The extra money will help families and businesses with the cost of living.
The country also borrows money, like a big loan. It costs more to pay back than before. Some people say the banks should give more. Others say they should not. The government decided they should, for now.
levels.why: It helps pay for the things everyone uses, like schools and hospitals.

headline: Burnham heads to Brussels for 20 November summit as talk of rejoining the EU grows

terms.meaning: A scheme that puts a price on carbon pollution by making firms buy permits.
A fee on imports made with high carbon pollution.
To become a full member of the European Union again.

levels.headline: Burnham heads to Brussels for 20 November summit as talk of rejoining the EU grows
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will attend a UK-EU summit in Brussels on 20 November, where he will meet European Council President António Costa and Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Downing Street says the meeting will review progress since the May 2025 partnership and cover security, illegal migration and cutting red tape for farmers and food businesses.
Items on the table include a food and drink trade deal, a deal on emissions trading, progress towards linking energy systems, a youth experience scheme and deeper cooperation on immigration. A draft reportedly points to linking the UK and EU emissions trading systems, which could exempt goods from both sides' carbon border charges, though the draft could change.
Mr Burnham says the status quo is not good enough and that a serious conversation about long-term options should follow a successful summit. He has not ruled out negotiations on full EU membership. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the UK should first join existing EU defence frameworks and that the sides were not yet at the point of membership talks.
levels.why: The summit could change trade, travel and energy costs, and it frames the debate on how close Britain should be to the EU.

levels.headline: UK and EU prepare for 20 November summit amid debate over closer ties
levels.body:
Andy Burnham will travel to Brussels on 20 November for a UK-EU summit with António Costa and Ursula von der Leyen. The government says it will review progress since the May 2025 partnership, focusing on security, illegal migration and reducing red tape for farmers and food firms.
Possible agreements include a food and drink trade deal, linking the two sides' emissions trading systems, closer energy links, a youth experience scheme and more cooperation on immigration. A draft suggests the carbon-market link could exempt UK and EU goods from each other's carbon border charges, but it may still change.
The Prime Minister says the current relationship is not good enough and that a longer discussion about options should follow. He has not ruled out talks on rejoining the EU. Kaja Kallas, the EU's foreign policy chief, said the UK should first join existing defence frameworks and that membership talks would be difficult.
levels.why: It could cut costs for businesses and shapes the long-term question of Britain's place in Europe.

levels.headline: Prime Minister to meet EU leaders in Brussels on 20 November
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will meet EU leaders in Brussels on 20 November. He will see António Costa and Ursula von der Leyen. The government says the summit will look at what has been achieved since a May 2025 partnership, and talk about security, illegal migration and less paperwork for farmers and food businesses.
The two sides may agree a trade deal on food and drink, a link between their carbon pricing schemes, a youth experience scheme and more cooperation on migration. A draft says goods from each side could be spared the other's carbon border charges. The draft could change before the summit.
Mr Burnham says staying as things are is not good enough. He wants a serious talk about the long-term relationship after the summit and has not ruled out negotiating a return to the EU. The EU's Kaja Kallas said the UK should first join defence schemes and that talks on membership would be hard.
levels.why: Any deal could affect prices, trade and travel, and fuels the argument about rejoining.

levels.headline: UK and EU leaders to meet in Brussels to try to improve trade and cooperation
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, will go to Brussels on 20 November to meet the leaders of the European Union. The aim is to build on a partnership agreed in May 2025. The talks cover security, illegal migration and cutting red tape for farmers and food firms.
The sides may agree a deal on food and drink trade, link their carbon pricing systems, start a youth experience scheme and work together more on migration. Linking the carbon systems could mean goods are not charged extra carbon fees at each other's borders. This is only in a draft.
Mr Burnham says the way things are now is not good enough. After the summit, he wants a serious talk about options, and he has not ruled out discussing rejoining the EU. The EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said the UK should first join EU defence plans.
levels.why: Deals could make trade easier, and the bigger question is how close the UK should be to the EU.

levels.headline: Britain and the EU will meet to talk about working more closely together
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, will visit Brussels on 20 November. He will meet the top leaders of the European Union. The UK left the EU in 2020, but the two sides have been working on a new partnership since May 2025.
They will talk about safety, people crossing the sea illegally, and less paperwork for farmers and food firms. They may agree on trade in food and drink. They may also link their schemes that put a price on pollution. That could stop extra pollution charges on goods crossing the border. A youth scheme could let young people live and work abroad.
Mr Burnham says things as they are now are not good enough. He wants a big talk about the future afterwards. He has not ruled out rejoining the EU. An EU leader said the UK should first join EU defence plans.
levels.why: It could make trade easier and keep alive the question of whether Britain should rejoin.

levels.headline: Britain and Europe meet to talk about being better friends
levels.body:
The UK used to be in a group of countries called the European Union, or EU. It left in 2020. This is called Brexit. Now the leaders want to work together more. On 20 November, the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, will go to Brussels to meet the EU's bosses.
They will talk about keeping people safe, about people crossing the sea in boats, and about trade. They might agree to make it easier to sell food and drink. They might also agree a plan for charging firms for pollution that works in both places.
Mr Burnham says the way things are now is not good enough. He has not said no to the idea of rejoining. An EU leader said it is too early.
levels.why: It could make buying and selling things easier, and it keeps alive a big question about Brexit.

levels.headline: The UK and Europe want to work together more
levels.body:
The UK used to belong to a club of European countries called the EU. In 2020 it left. That is called Brexit. Now the UK leader, Andy Burnham, wants to work more closely with the EU again.
On 20 November he will go to Brussels, where the EU has its main offices, to talk to its leaders. They will talk about trade, safety, and young people living in each other's countries. Trade means buying and selling things across borders. They might make food and drink easier to sell. They might also share rules about pollution.
Mr Burnham says things now are not good enough. He has not said no to rejoining the EU one day. Some EU leaders say it is too soon.
levels.why: It might change what things cost and how easy it is to travel and trade.

levels.headline: The UK and Europe meet to talk about being friends again
levels.body:
The UK used to be in a group with many other European countries. The group is called the EU. The UK left it in 2020, and that is called Brexit. Now the UK leader wants to be closer to the EU again.
He is called the Prime Minister. His name is Andy Burnham. He is going to a city called Brussels on 20 November to meet the EU leaders. They will talk about being safe and about selling things to each other. They might make it easier to sell food and drink.
Some people want the UK to join the EU again. Others do not. The Prime Minister has not said no. An EU leader said it is too early to talk about that.
levels.why: It might change what things cost and how easy it is to trade with our neighbours.

levels.headline: Two neighbours meet to talk about getting closer
levels.body:
Imagine two schools that used to share one playground. One day one school decided to build its own playground. Now they live next door but do not share any more. The UK and the EU are a bit like those schools.
The UK left the EU in 2020. The leader of the UK, Andy Burnham, is going to meet the EU's leaders on 20 November. They will talk about sharing things like keeping people safe, and selling food and drink to each other.
Some people want the UK to go back to the EU. Others do not. Mr Burnham has not said no. An EU leader said it is too soon to talk about that.
levels.why: It could change what things cost and how easily we can work with our neighbours.

levels.headline: Next-door neighbours meet to talk about sharing
levels.body:
Imagine two neighbours who used to share a garden. One day they stopped sharing. Now they want to talk about whether they could share again.
The UK is one neighbour. The EU, which is a group of many countries, is the other. The UK left the group a few years ago. The UK's leader, Andy Burnham, is going to meet the other leaders on 20 November.
They will talk about being safe, and about swapping things, such as food and drink. Some grown-ups would like the UK to join the group again. Others do not. Nobody has decided yet.
levels.why: It is about how neighbours can work together and share.

headline: Democrats win control of both chambers of Congress in midterm rejection of Trump

terms.meaning: US elections held halfway through a president's four-year term.
A Senate rule that usually needs 60 votes to pass most laws.
A president's power to block a law passed by Congress.

levels.headline: Democrats win control of both chambers of Congress in midterm rejection of Trump
levels.body:
Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate in the US midterm elections on 3 November, giving them a majority in each chamber for the final two years of President Donald Trump's term. Counts were still continuing, so seat totals vary by source.
CNBC's election desk projected Democrats at at least 250 House seats, and on track for at least 54 Senate seats, with gains in states including Texas, Ohio, Kansas and Maine. A Mississippi Senate race was still very close. Euronews said the result reflected anger over living costs, tariffs and the war against Iran.
Mr Trump told the New York Times he was absolutely willing to accept the results and told Fox News he plans to use his veto. Democrats lack the two-thirds majorities needed to override a veto and will fall short of the 60 Senate votes needed to beat the filibuster on most laws. They are expected to launch investigations into the Iran war, immigration enforcement and corruption allegations, and to block appointments.
levels.why: Control of Congress limits what the president can pass, and it can change US policy on trade, war and spending.

levels.headline: Democrats take both houses of Congress in a sweeping midterm result
levels.body:
Democrats won both the House of Representatives and the Senate on 3 November, handing them a majority in each chamber for Donald Trump's last two years. Some counts are unfinished.
CNBC projected at least 250 House seats and at least 54 Senate seats for Democrats, who flipped seats in Texas, Ohio, Kansas, Maine and elsewhere. The Mississippi Senate race was too close to call. Euronews reported anger over living costs, tariffs and the war with Iran as drivers of the result.
Mr Trump said he would accept the results and also said he plans to use his veto power. Democrats cannot override a veto without Republican help, and they remain short of 60 Senate votes to bypass the filibuster. They are expected to investigate the Iran war, immigration enforcement and corruption allegations, and to block Mr Trump's agenda and senior appointments.
levels.why: It will change what the White House can achieve and may affect markets, trade and foreign policy.

levels.headline: Democrats win control of the US Congress
levels.body:
The Democratic Party has won control of both parts of the US Congress, the House of Representatives and the Senate, in elections held on 3 November. These are called the midterms because they take place halfway through a president's term. Counting is not finished.
CNBC says Democrats will have at least 250 House seats and at least 54 Senate seats. They won seats in states including Texas and Ohio. One Senate race in Mississippi is very close. Euronews says voters were angry about living costs, tariffs and the war with Iran.
President Trump says he accepts the result but plans to use his veto, which lets him block laws. Democrats do not have enough votes to overrule him. They also cannot beat the Senate rule that needs 60 votes for most laws. They are expected to investigate the Iran war and immigration enforcement.
levels.why: It limits the president's power and could change US policy.

levels.headline: Democrats take control of both houses of the US Congress
levels.body:
Voters in the United States have given the Democratic Party control of both houses of Congress, the House of Representatives and the Senate. The vote was on 3 November, halfway through President Donald Trump's four-year term. Counting is still going on.
Democrats are projected to hold at least 250 of the 435 House seats and at least 54 Senate seats. They won seats in places like Texas, Ohio and Maine. News reports say many voters were unhappy about prices, tariffs and the war with Iran.
Mr Trump says he accepts the result but will use his veto to block laws he dislikes. Democrats do not have enough votes to overrule a veto. They are expected to hold investigations into the Iran war and immigration enforcement.
levels.why: It means the president cannot easily pass new laws, and it may shift US policy.

levels.headline: Democrats win big in US elections and take over Congress
levels.body:
Voters in the United States held elections on 3 November. The Democratic Party won control of both parts of Congress, which is where US laws are made. The two parts are called the House and the Senate. Counting is not quite finished.
The elections were halfway through the term of President Donald Trump, who is a Republican. Many voters were unhappy about high prices, taxes on imports called tariffs, and the war with Iran. Democrats won seats in several states, including Texas and Ohio.
The president says he accepts the result. But he also says he will use his veto, which means he can say no to a law. Democrats do not have enough votes to overrule him. They plan to ask hard questions about the war and other things.
levels.why: It means the president has less power to do what he wants.

levels.headline: Democrats win control of the US parliament
levels.body:
In the United States, the group that makes the laws is called Congress. Voters chose who should be in it on 3 November. The Democratic Party won most seats in both parts of Congress. Counting is still going on.
President Donald Trump is from the Republican Party. He is the head of the government. But he cannot make laws on his own. Congress must agree. Now the other party is in charge of Congress. Many voters said they were unhappy about prices and the war with Iran.
The president says he accepts the result. But he says he will say no to laws he does not like. Democrats do not have enough votes to overrule him. They will also ask questions about the war.
levels.why: The president will find it harder to get his plans passed.

levels.headline: US voters choose a new team in charge of lawmaking
levels.body:
In America, the people who make the laws are called Congress. Voters pick them. On 3 November there was a vote. The Democratic Party, one of the two main teams, won most seats. They now control the whole of Congress.
The President, Donald Trump, belongs to the other team, the Republicans. He is in charge of the country. But he needs Congress to agree to new laws. Now the other team has the most votes in Congress. Many voters said they were unhappy about prices and about a war with Iran.
The President says he accepts the result. But he can still say no to a law. This is called a veto. The other team does not have enough votes to overrule it.
levels.why: The President will find it harder to get his ideas turned into laws.

levels.headline: The other team wins the vote in America
levels.body:
America has a president. He is called Donald Trump. He is the leader of the country. But he cannot make laws on his own. A group called Congress has to agree. People vote to choose who sits in Congress.
This week people voted. The other team, called the Democrats, won most seats. The president's team, called the Republicans, lost. Many voters said things cost too much. Some were unhappy about a war.
The president says he accepts the result. He can still say no to new laws. The Democrats will ask the president hard questions. Everyone will watch what happens next.
levels.why: It changes who has the power to make rules in America.

levels.headline: A class vote has a surprise winner
levels.body:
Imagine a class has a leader. The leader is the class captain. The captain can suggest ideas. But the class must vote on them. This is like how America works, with a president and a group of lawmakers.
This week, the class voted for the group of lawmakers. The team that does not agree with the captain won. Many children said they were unhappy that things cost too much.
The captain says he accepts the vote. But he can still say no to some ideas. The new team will ask the captain questions. It will be harder for the captain to get all his ideas passed.
levels.why: It means the leader has to listen more.

levels.headline: Voting for who makes the rules
levels.body:
Imagine a school where the pupils vote for a council. The council decides some rules. The headteacher also has a say, but the council has power too. America works a bit like that.
This week American grown-ups voted. The team that did not agree with the president won most seats. That means the president will find it harder to get his own way.
Many voters said they were unhappy about things costing too much. The winning team says it will ask the president lots of questions. The president says he will say no to rules he does not like.
levels.why: It decides who has power to make the rules.

headline: US economy adds 165,000 jobs in October, far above forecasts, as unemployment slips to 4.1%

terms.meaning: The number of paid jobs in the economy.
The share of people looking for work who cannot find it.
The US central bank, which sets interest rates.

levels.headline: US economy adds 165,000 jobs in October, far above forecasts, as unemployment slips to 4.1%
levels.body:
The US economy added 165,000 jobs in October, well above the consensus forecast of about 59,000, according to figures released on 6 November. The unemployment rate edged down to 4.1% from a forecast of 4.2%. Gains came in professional and business services, healthcare and manufacturing, and figures for August and September were revised up.
Average hourly earnings rose 0.4% on the month and 3.1% over the year. There were weaker signs under the surface: a broader measure of unemployment, which includes discouraged workers and people in part-time jobs who want full-time work, rose 0.3 percentage points to 7.9%. The average length of unemployment jumped to 27.1 weeks, the highest since September 2021.
The 10-year Treasury yield rose after the report. Investors judged that it strengthens the case for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again at its meeting next month, with inflation still above its 2% target.
levels.why: Strong jobs data can push up interest rates, which affects borrowing costs well beyond the US.

levels.headline: October jobs report beats forecasts and raises odds of another Fed rate rise
levels.body:
US employers added 165,000 jobs in October, far more than the roughly 59,000 economists expected. The unemployment rate fell slightly to 4.1%. The report came out on 6 November. Professional services, healthcare and manufacturing led the gains, and earlier months were revised higher.
Pay rose 0.4% in the month and 3.1% over the year. But a broader unemployment measure rose to 7.9%, and the typical time spent jobless reached 27.1 weeks, the longest since September 2021, so the picture is not all positive.
Government bond yields rose and investors now see a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to lift interest rates in December, because inflation remains above the bank's 2% target.
levels.why: A strong labour market makes the Fed less likely to cut rates and more likely to raise them.

levels.headline: US employers add far more jobs than expected in October
levels.body:
American employers created 165,000 new jobs in October. Experts had expected only about 59,000. The unemployment rate dipped to 4.1%. The figures came out on 6 November. Most new jobs were in business services, healthcare and factories. The numbers for August and September were also raised.
Wages grew 0.4% in the month and 3.1% over the year. Still, there were worrying signs. A wider measure of unemployment rose to 7.9%. People who are out of work are taking longer to find jobs, on average 27.1 weeks, the longest since September 2021.
After the report, investors thought the Federal Reserve might raise interest rates again at its next meeting, in December. Prices are still rising faster than the bank's 2% goal.
levels.why: Interest rates in the US influence borrowing costs and share prices worldwide.

levels.headline: US adds many more jobs than expected in October
levels.body:
The US economy created 165,000 jobs in October. Experts had guessed about 59,000. The share of people looking for work who could not find it fell a little, to 4.1%. The numbers were published on 6 November. New jobs were mostly in business services, healthcare and factories.
Pay went up 0.4% in the month and 3.1% over the year. But some signs were less good. A wider measure of people without enough work rose to 7.9%. People out of work now take 27.1 weeks on average to find a job, the longest since September 2021.
Investors now think the Federal Reserve, the US central bank, may raise interest rates again in December. Prices are still rising faster than the bank wants, which is 2% a year.
levels.why: A strong jobs market can lead to higher interest rates.

levels.headline: More Americans found jobs than experts expected
levels.body:
The US had a strong month for jobs in October. Employers added 165,000 new jobs. Experts had thought it would be only about 59,000. The share of people without a job fell to 4.1%. This was announced on 6 November.
Most new jobs were in healthcare, business services and factories. Pay went up a little too. But it was not all good news. More people are working part-time when they want full-time work. People who lose their jobs are taking longer to find new ones, more than 27 weeks on average.
Because the jobs news was strong, some investors think the Federal Reserve, which sets US interest rates, may raise them again in December. Prices are still rising too fast for the bank.
levels.why: Strong jobs can lead to higher interest rates, which affect loans.

levels.headline: A strong month for jobs in America
levels.body:
America had a good month for jobs in October. Employers hired 165,000 more people. Experts had only expected about 59,000. Out of every 100 people who wanted to work, about four could not find a job. That is a low number.
Many of the new jobs were in hospitals, offices and factories. Wages also went up. But some people are finding it hard. Those who lose a job now wait a long time to find a new one, over six months on average.
The news may lead the bank that sets American interest rates to raise them again in December. When interest rates go up, borrowing gets more expensive. Prices are still going up faster than the bank wants.
levels.why: It can change what borrowing costs in the US and beyond.

levels.headline: More people in America got jobs last month
levels.body:
Last month in America, many more people got jobs than experts thought. Employers hired 165,000 people. The experts had guessed about 59,000. About four in every 100 people who wanted a job could not find one.
New jobs came in hospitals, offices and factories. Wages went up a little. But finding a job is slow for some people. If you lose your job, it can take more than six months to find a new one.
Because the news was good, the bank that sets America's interest rates may raise them again in December. This is the Federal Reserve. Higher rates make loans cost more. Prices are still going up too fast.
levels.why: It may change how much loans cost.

levels.headline: America found lots of new jobs last month
levels.body:
Many people in America got new jobs last month. Employers hired 165,000 more workers. Experts had thought it would be much fewer. About four in every 100 people who wanted work could not find it.
The new jobs were in hospitals, offices and factories. Workers also got paid a little more. Some people still find it hard to get a new job after losing one. It can take over six months.
A big bank in America looks at jobs to decide on interest rates. Because there were lots of jobs, it may raise rates in December. That makes loans cost more.
levels.why: It may make loans cost more.

levels.headline: Lots of new jobs for grown-ups
levels.body:
Grown-ups go to work to earn money. In America last month, many more grown-ups found work than people expected. It was 165,000 more jobs. They work in places like hospitals, offices and factories.
Some people still find it hard to get a job. When they lose one, it can take over six months to find another. That is a long time.
A bank in America looks at jobs when it decides about interest rates. Interest is the extra you pay back on a loan. With so many jobs, the bank may make it bigger in December.
levels.why: It tells us how well grown-ups are doing at finding work.

levels.headline: More grown-ups have jobs
levels.body:
Many grown-ups go to work to earn money. They might work in a hospital, a shop or a factory. In America last month, lots more grown-ups found jobs than anyone guessed.
It is like when a class expects five new pupils to join and fifty join instead. That is a nice surprise. But some grown-ups still find it hard to find work after losing a job. It can take months.
A bank in America watches how many people have jobs. If lots of people have jobs, it may make borrowing cost more. This is to stop prices rising too fast.
levels.why: It shows how many families have money coming in.

headline: US launches limited strikes on Iran as Trump claims progress in Qatar-mediated talks

terms.meaning: A narrow sea passage in the Gulf used for a large share of the world's oil.
A third party that helps two sides reach agreement.
Penalties, usually economic, imposed on a country.

levels.headline: US launches limited strikes on Iran as Trump claims progress in Qatar-mediated talks
levels.body:
US forces carried out limited strikes in southern Iran on Friday night, which President Donald Trump called minor, even as he said the United States had made a lot of progress in talks with Tehran. Qatar, which is mediating, said on Saturday that negotiations continue and denied reports that the sides had failed to reach a deal.
A senior Iranian official said Iran had submitted a nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatar, but that discussions depended on the US first meeting seven Iranian demands, which include sanctions relief, access to frozen assets and war reparations. Washington insists nuclear issues must be part of the initial talks. Iran has said it can reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the US accepts its conditions.
Iranian media suggested later blasts were Iranian military activity rather than US strikes, and both sides have continued to hit ships in the Strait. The war began when the US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February. Analysts are split: one puts the chance of fighting resuming at 80%, while others see the end of the US midterms as a possible opening for diplomacy.
levels.why: The war has pushed up energy prices and inflation worldwide, so a deal or a collapse of talks affects living costs.

levels.headline: US carries out new strikes on Iran while talks via Qatar go on
levels.body:
The United States carried out limited strikes in southern Iran on Friday night. President Donald Trump described them as minor and said the US had made a lot of progress in talks with Tehran. Qatar, the mediator, said on Saturday that negotiations continue and denied that they had failed.
A senior Iranian official said Tehran had sent a nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatar. Iran says talks depend on the US first meeting seven demands, including sanctions relief, frozen assets and reparations. Washington wants nuclear issues dealt with at the start. Iran says it could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if its conditions are met.
Iranian media suggested later explosions were Iranian military activity, not US attacks, and both sides continue to strike vessels in the Strait. The war began on 28 February. Analysts disagree on what comes next, with one seeing an 80% chance fighting resumes.
levels.why: Whether the talks succeed will influence oil prices, inflation and interest rates around the world.

levels.headline: US strikes Iran again as both sides say talks are still alive
levels.body:
The United States carried out limited attacks in southern Iran on Friday night. President Donald Trump called them minor and said there had been a lot of progress in talks with Iran. Qatar, which is helping the two sides talk, said on Saturday that the talks go on.
An Iranian official said Iran had sent a nuclear proposal through Qatar. But Iran says it wants the US to meet seven demands first, such as lifting sanctions, releasing frozen money and paying for war damage. The US says nuclear issues must be part of the first talks. Iran says it could reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for oil, within two days if its conditions are met.
The war started on 28 February when the US and Israel attacked Iran. Ships in the Strait are still being hit. Experts are divided on whether fighting will start again.
levels.why: The war affects oil, petrol prices and inflation everywhere.

levels.headline: US hits Iran again, but talks to end the war carry on
levels.body:
The United States carried out limited strikes in southern Iran on Friday night. President Donald Trump called them minor. He also said that talks with Iran were making a lot of progress. Qatar is helping to pass messages between the two sides. It said on Saturday that the talks go on.
Iran says it has sent a proposal about its nuclear programme. But it wants the US first to meet seven demands. These include ending sanctions, freeing frozen money and paying for war damage. The US wants nuclear issues discussed first. Iran says it could reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for oil ships, within two days of a deal.
The war began on 28 February. Ships are still being hit in the Strait. Experts disagree about what will happen next.
levels.why: It affects oil prices, and so the cost of fuel and energy for everyone.

levels.headline: The US and Iran keep talking, even as the US hits Iran again
levels.body:
The United States has hit places in the south of Iran. This happened on Friday night. President Donald Trump said the attacks were small. He also said talks with Iran were going well. A country called Qatar is helping the two sides to talk. It said on Saturday that the talks have not ended.
Iran says it has sent a plan about its nuclear work. But Iran wants the US to agree to seven things first. They include ending sanctions, which are rules that hurt its trade, and paying for war damage. The US wants to talk about nuclear work first. Iran says it could reopen a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz, which oil ships use, within two days.
The war began on 28 February. Experts do not agree on what will happen next.
levels.why: The war makes oil and fuel more expensive for many families.

levels.headline: The US hits Iran, but talks to end the war go on
levels.body:
There is a war involving the United States and Iran. It began on 28 February. The US attacked Iran again on Friday night. The American president, Donald Trump, said the attack was small. He also said talks were going well. A country called Qatar helps them speak to each other.
Iran says it wants some things before the talks go further. It wants the US to lift rules that stop it trading. It wants frozen money back, and money for damage. The US wants to talk about Iran's nuclear work first. Iran says it could open a key sea route for oil ships within two days of a deal.
It is hard to say what will happen next. Some experts think the fighting will start again.
levels.why: The war pushes up the price of oil and fuel for everyone.

levels.headline: A war between America and Iran is still not over
levels.body:
America and Iran have been fighting since 28 February. This week, America attacked Iran again, but only a little. The American president, Donald Trump, said the attack was small. Both countries say they are still talking. A small country called Qatar helps them to talk.
Iran wants some things first. It wants the other side to stop its rules that hurt Iran's trade, and to give back money that is frozen. Iran also says it could open a sea road for oil ships within two days.
Why does this matter? Much of the world's oil goes through that sea road. When it is blocked, petrol and energy cost more. Some experts think the fighting will start again.
levels.why: It affects what we pay for petrol and energy.

levels.headline: Two sides keep talking even while still arguing
levels.body:
Two countries, America and Iran, are in a war that started in February. This week, America sent in a small attack. But both sides also say they are still talking. A friend country, Qatar, helps them talk.
Each side wants something before it will agree. Iran wants America to stop rules that hurt Iran's money and to give back some frozen money. America wants to talk about Iran's nuclear work. Iran also says it could open a blocked sea road for ships carrying oil.
The war matters to people far away. Oil costs more when ships cannot move. That makes petrol and heating cost more.
levels.why: It affects the price of petrol and heating.

levels.headline: Two sides argue but keep talking
levels.body:
Imagine two children have an argument that has gone on for months. Each wants the other to say sorry first. A friend tries to help them talk. That is a bit like what is happening between America and Iran.
They have been in a war since February. This week, America made a small attack. But both said they still want to talk. A friend country, Qatar, is in the middle, passing messages.
Why does it matter? Oil ships pass through a narrow sea road near Iran. The war stopped some of them. When oil is hard to get, petrol and heating cost more for everyone.
levels.why: It can change the price of petrol and energy for families.

levels.headline: Friends try to help two sides stop arguing
levels.body:
Imagine two children are cross with each other. They are having a very big argument. A friend tries to help. The friend runs between them with messages. That is a bit like Qatar, which is helping America and Iran.
The two countries have been fighting since February. This week there was another small attack. But they both said they would keep talking. Each wants something before it will agree.
The fight matters to everyone, because oil ships are stuck. When oil is hard to get, it costs more. That means petrol and heating cost more, too.
levels.why: It may make petrol and heating cost more.

headline: Brent crude settles at $98.32 after a week of swings driven by Iran diplomacy

terms.meaning: The main international benchmark price for oil, quoted per barrel.
A unit of oil, about 159 litres.
The final price at the close of trading.

levels.headline: Brent crude settles at $98.32 after a week of swings driven by Iran diplomacy
levels.body:
Brent crude futures, the international oil benchmark, settled at $98.32 a barrel on Friday 6 November, up 3 cents on the day. Oil fell over the week as investors weighed the risk of conflict with Iran after the US midterm elections.
The week was volatile. Brent lost 7.6% on 2 November to settle at $104.77 on hopes of diplomacy, then fell to $94.62 on 4 November, a near two-month low, before recovering to around $96 to $97 on 5 November. Reports that Iran had sent a nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatar drove much of the movement. Brent is about 54.5% higher than a year ago.
Analysts are split. Rapidan Energy Group's Bob McNally puts the chance of military fighting resuming at 80% and says both main benchmarks could rise above $100 a barrel. Trading Economics forecasts about $100.92 by the end of the quarter. The war began on 28 February and has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
levels.why: Oil prices feed into petrol, heating bills and inflation, so swings affect household costs and interest rate decisions.

levels.headline: Oil ends a volatile week near $98 a barrel as markets watch US-Iran talks
levels.body:
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, closed Friday 6 November at $98.32 a barrel, a rise of 3 cents. It finished the week lower as traders weighed the chance of renewed conflict with Iran after the midterms.
Early in the week Brent fell 7.6% to $104.77 on hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough, then dropped to $94.62 on 4 November, its lowest in almost two months, before bouncing to about $96 to $97. Reports of an Iranian nuclear proposal sent through Qatar were a big influence. The price is still about 54.5% above a year ago.
Rapidan Energy Group's Bob McNally sees an 80% probability that fighting resumes, which could push prices above $100. Trading Economics projects about $100.92 by the end of this quarter. The Iran war has disrupted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz since February.
levels.why: Higher oil feeds through to fuel and energy bills and can keep inflation and interest rates high.

levels.headline: Oil price ends a wild week close to $98 a barrel
levels.body:
The price of Brent crude, a main world oil price, finished Friday 6 November at $98.32 a barrel. That was up 3 cents on the day. For the week, oil prices fell as traders weighed the risk of fighting with Iran.
On 2 November the price dropped 7.6% to $104.77 on hopes of talks. On 4 November it fell to $94.62, the lowest in almost two months. Then it rose again to around $96 or $97. News that Iran had sent a nuclear plan to the US through Qatar moved the price. It is still about 54.5% higher than a year ago.
One expert, Bob McNally, thinks there is an 80% chance that fighting will start again. He says prices could go above $100. Another forecaster expects about $100.92 by the end of the quarter.
levels.why: Oil prices change what we pay for petrol and heating.

levels.headline: Oil prices swing wildly as markets watch Iran
levels.body:
The price of oil ended last week at $98.32 a barrel for Brent, the main world price. It had a bumpy week. On Monday it fell 7.6% to $104.77 because people hoped for peace talks. By Wednesday it was $94.62, the lowest in almost two months.
Then it went up again. News that Iran had sent a nuclear plan to the US through Qatar moved the price up and down. Oil is still about 54.5% more expensive than a year ago. The war with Iran began in February and has made it harder to ship oil through a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz.
One expert says there is an 80% chance that fighting will start again, which could push the price above $100. Others hope for a deal.
levels.why: Higher oil prices mean dearer petrol and energy, and can keep prices rising.

levels.headline: Oil costs a lot, and the price keeps jumping
levels.body:
Oil is used to make petrol, diesel and many other things. A barrel of the main world kind, called Brent, cost $98.32 on Friday 6 November. That is about 54% more than a year ago. During the week the price jumped around a lot.
It fell on Monday to $104.77 when people hoped America and Iran would agree to talk. It fell again to $94.62 on Wednesday. Then it rose a bit. A war with Iran, which began in February, has made it harder to move oil by ship through a narrow sea route.
One expert thinks fighting will start again and the price could go above $100. Others hope a deal will bring it down.
levels.why: Oil affects how much petrol and heating cost for families.

levels.headline: Oil costs a lot and its price keeps changing
levels.body:
Oil is used to make petrol for cars. It is also used for heating and to make plastic. The price of oil changes every day. On Friday, a barrel of the main world kind cost $98.32. That is more than it was a year ago.
The price went up and down this week. It fell when people hoped the war with Iran would end. It went up when people feared it would go on. A war can make oil more expensive, because ships find it hard to carry the oil.
