One expert thinks the price could go above $100 if the fighting starts again. Others hope for peace and cheaper oil.
levels.why: Dearer oil can mean higher petrol prices and higher bills.

levels.headline: The price of oil goes up and down
levels.body:
Oil is a black liquid from under the ground. We use it to make petrol for cars. It is also used for heating. People buy and sell oil all over the world. The price changes every day.
This week one barrel cost about $98. It is higher than last year. It went up and down a lot. When people thought the war between America and Iran might end, the price fell. When they thought it might get worse, the price rose.
If oil costs more, petrol costs more too. Some people think the price may go above $100. Others think it will fall.
levels.why: It affects the cost of petrol and heating.

levels.headline: Oil is dearer and bounces about
levels.body:
Oil is a liquid found under the ground. People use it to make petrol for cars and fuel for planes. It costs a lot of money. This week it cost about $98 for one big barrel. That is more than last year.
The price went up and down this week. When people hoped for peace between two countries, the price went down. When they worried about more fighting, it went up. Ships carry oil. A war can stop the ships.
If oil costs more, petrol costs more too. That makes it dearer to get around.
levels.why: It changes what families pay for petrol.

levels.headline: Why petrol can cost more
levels.body:
Imagine you sell lemonade. If lemons become hard to find, they cost more. Then your lemonade costs more too. Oil is a bit like the lemons. It is used to make petrol.
This week oil cost a lot. It was about $98 for one big barrel. The price went up and down. There is a war far away, and ships find it hard to carry oil. When ships cannot move, there is less oil to buy.
If oil costs more, petrol costs more too. Grown-ups pay more to drive. People hope the war will end and the price will drop.
levels.why: It decides how much grown-ups pay for petrol.

levels.headline: Why things cost more when something is hard to find
levels.body:
Imagine a sweet shop. If the shop runs out of your favourite sweets, other shoppers still want them. The shop can ask for more money. Oil works in a similar way. If there is less oil to buy, it costs more.
This week, oil cost a lot of money, about $98 for a big barrel. A war far away has made it hard to ship oil. When ships cannot carry it, there is less to buy.
Oil is used to make petrol. If oil costs more, petrol costs more. Grown-ups pay more to drive cars. Everyone hopes the war ends soon.
levels.why: It explains why petrol can cost more.

headline: Israel's president tasks Netanyahu rival Eisenkot with forming a government

terms.meaning: Israel's parliament, which has 120 seats.
A group of parties that join together to form a government.
The formal authority to try to form a government.

levels.headline: Israel's president tasks Netanyahu rival Eisenkot with forming a government
levels.body:
Israel's president, Isaac Herzog, has asked opposition figure Gadi Eisenkot to try to form the next government, a setback for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. After consultations, factions with 67 members of the Knesset backed Mr Eisenkot, against 46 for Mr Netanyahu, the president's office said.
Neither bloc has a majority after last month's election. Mr Netanyahu's bloc won 53 seats and Mr Eisenkot's 48, short of the 61 needed in the 120-seat Knesset. Likud remained the largest party, and Arab parties won a record 19 seats between them, making them potential kingmakers. Mr Eisenkot's allies largely resist relying on them, and he could try for a minority government with outside support, which others in his bloc have said they would reject.
Mr Eisenkot has 28 days to form a government, extendable by 14. If he fails, the president can offer the mandate to someone else, and a new election could follow. Mr Netanyahu called for a national unity government and alleged Arab parties stole the vote, but the election commission found no fraud.
levels.why: The outcome will shape Israel's approach to the war in Gaza and the wider region.

levels.headline: Eisenkot given first chance to form Israel's next government
levels.body:
President Isaac Herzog has given opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot the first chance to build a coalition, after factions representing 67 MPs backed him against 46 for Benjamin Netanyahu.
Nobody has a majority. Mr Netanyahu's bloc won 53 of the 120 Knesset seats and Mr Eisenkot's won 48, with 61 needed. Likud is still the biggest party, and Arab parties won a record 19 seats between them. Mr Eisenkot's allies mostly do not want to depend on them, and some reject a minority government supported from outside.
He has 28 days, which can be extended by 14. If he cannot succeed, the mandate may go to someone else, or Israel may go back to the polls. Mr Netanyahu wants a national unity government and says Arab parties stole the election, though the election commission found no evidence of fraud.
levels.why: A new government would set Israel's direction on Gaza, the Iran war and relations with the US.

levels.headline: Israel's president picks Netanyahu's rival to try to form a government
levels.body:
Israel's president, Isaac Herzog, has asked Gadi Eisenkot to try to form the next government. This is a setback for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Parties with 67 members of parliament backed Mr Eisenkot, and parties with 46 backed Mr Netanyahu.
The election did not give anyone a majority. Mr Netanyahu's group won 53 seats and Mr Eisenkot's won 48. To rule, a group needs 61 of the 120 seats. Arab parties won a record 19 seats, so they could decide the outcome. But Mr Eisenkot's allies do not want to rely on them.
Mr Eisenkot has 28 days, and can ask for 14 more. If he fails, someone else may get a turn, or there may be another election. Mr Netanyahu says Arab parties stole the vote. The election commission found no fraud.
levels.why: The new government will decide Israel's choices on the Gaza war and the region.

levels.headline: Netanyahu's rival is asked to try to form Israel's new government
levels.body:
Israel's president has asked Gadi Eisenkot, a rival of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, to try to form the next government. Parties with 67 of the 120 seats in the parliament backed Mr Eisenkot. Parties with 46 seats backed Mr Netanyahu.
Last month's election did not give either side a majority. A group needs 61 seats to govern. Mr Netanyahu's side won 53 and Mr Eisenkot's side won 48. Arab parties won a record 19 seats, so they could be very important. But many of Mr Eisenkot's allies do not want to depend on them.
He has 28 days to form a government and can ask for 14 more. If he fails, the president could pick someone else, or Israel could hold a new election. Mr Netanyahu says the election was stolen, but the election commission found no fraud.
levels.why: It affects who leads Israel and how it deals with its neighbours.

levels.headline: Israel asks Netanyahu's rival to try to lead the next government
levels.body:
Israel held an election last month, but no one won enough seats to rule alone. Now Israel's president, Isaac Herzog, has asked a rival of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, called Gadi Eisenkot, to try to build a government. More politicians backed Mr Eisenkot, 67, than Mr Netanyahu, 46.
To govern, a group of parties needs 61 of the 120 seats in parliament. Mr Netanyahu's group won 53 and Mr Eisenkot's group won 48. Arab parties won a record 19 seats. They could decide who wins, but many of Mr Eisenkot's allies do not want to rely on them.
Mr Eisenkot has 28 days, plus 14 more if needed. If he fails, there could be a new election. Mr Netanyahu says the election was stolen. The election commission says it found no fraud.
levels.why: It will decide who runs Israel, which is at the centre of a lot of world news.

levels.headline: Israel's leader may change after a close election
levels.body:
Israel had an election last month. No one won enough seats to rule alone. Now the president has asked a rival of the Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, to try to make a government. The rival is called Gadi Eisenkot.
To rule, a group of parties needs more than half of the 120 seats in parliament. That is 61. Mr Netanyahu's side won 53 and Mr Eisenkot's side won 48. Arab parties won a record 19. But Mr Eisenkot's friends do not want to depend on them.
Mr Eisenkot has 28 days to try. If he cannot, there might be another election. Mr Netanyahu says the election was stolen. A group that checks elections says it found no cheating.
levels.why: It could change the leader of Israel, which affects the whole region.

levels.headline: Who will lead Israel next?
levels.body:
Israel had an election last month. Nobody won enough seats. A leader needs more than half of the seats to rule. In Israel, that means 61 out of 120.
So the president asked a man called Gadi Eisenkot to try. He is a rival of the current leader, Benjamin Netanyahu. He must find enough parties to work with him. He has 28 days.
If he cannot do it, there might be another election. Mr Netanyahu says the election was unfair. A group that checked found no cheating.
levels.why: It decides who runs Israel.

levels.headline: Trying to build a team to lead a country
levels.body:
In Israel, people have just voted. No team won enough seats to lead on its own. A team needs 61 of the 120 seats. So parties must join up to form a team. That is called a coalition.
The president has asked a man called Gadi Eisenkot to try to build a team. He has 28 days. The old leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, would like to keep his job. He says the vote was not fair. A group that checked the vote says there was no cheating.
If Mr Eisenkot cannot build a team, there may be a new vote.
levels.why: It decides who runs a country that is often in the news.

levels.headline: Picking a team captain
levels.body:
Imagine a class is picking a team captain. No one gets enough votes to win. So the teacher asks one pupil to try to get other pupils to join their team. The pupil has a few weeks to do it.
That is a bit like what is happening in Israel. People voted, but no team had enough votes to lead. The president asked a man called Gadi Eisenkot to try to join teams together.
The old captain, Benjamin Netanyahu, wants to keep his job. If Mr Eisenkot cannot make a team, there may be another vote.
levels.why: It decides who will lead the country.

levels.headline: A tricky vote in a faraway country
levels.body:
Imagine your class is voting for a class captain. The vote is so close that no one wins by enough. So the teacher asks one child to try to get others to team up.
In Israel, people have voted for their leaders. It was very close. The president asked a man called Gadi Eisenkot to try to team up with other groups. He has about four weeks.
The old leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, wants to keep his job. If no team forms, they may vote again.
levels.why: It decides who will lead the country.

headline: Deadly Russian strike on Zaporizhzhia clouds Ukraine peace talks due in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November

terms.meaning: An attack followed by a second strike on the same place, often hitting rescuers.
To act as a go-between to help two sides reach agreement.
Negotiations between officials rather than between leaders.

levels.headline: Deadly Russian strike on Zaporizhzhia clouds Ukraine peace talks due in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November
levels.body:
A Russian attack on a humanitarian aid site in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region has killed 33 people, with more than 50 still missing, Euronews reported, as the United States prepares to mediate talks between Kyiv and Moscow in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November.
Early reports put the toll lower, at 24 including two rescue workers and four police officers, and figures have kept changing. Ukrainian officials said the site was a school. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that after the first aerial bomb there was a double-tap strike with nine more bombs. The Kremlin did not deny the accusations, and spokesman Dmitry Peskov called the practice completely normal in such situations.
US envoy Steve Witkoff said the United States will mediate working-level negotiations between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi, and Moscow has agreed to return to three-way talks. Mr Zelenskyy said the attack knocked hopes of progress towards peace. Russia also launched 289 drones and 17 ballistic missiles overnight at Ukraine on 3 November.
levels.why: The talks are a rare chance to move towards ending the war, and attacks on civilians test whether they can succeed.

levels.headline: Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi overshadowed by deadly Zaporizhzhia attack
levels.body:
Russian strikes on a humanitarian aid site in Zaporizhzhia have killed 33 people, with more than 50 missing. The attack comes days before US-mediated talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November.
Casualty figures have risen since early reports of at least 24. Ukrainian officials said the site was a school and President Zelenskyy said a second wave of nine bombs followed the first strike. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov described such tactics as completely normal in such situations and did not deny the accusations.
US envoy Steve Witkoff announced that the US will mediate working-level talks, and Moscow has agreed to attend three-way negotiations. Mr Zelenskyy said the strike damaged hopes of progress towards peace. Russia launched 289 drones and 17 ballistic missiles on 3 November.
levels.why: The outcome could affect the war, energy prices and European security.

levels.headline: Deadly Russian attack hits Ukrainian city days before peace talks
levels.body:
A Russian attack on an aid site in the Ukrainian region of Zaporizhzhia has killed 33 people. More than 50 people are still missing. The attack came a few days before talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November, which the United States will help to organise.
Early reports gave a lower toll, and the numbers have kept changing. Ukrainian officials said the site was a school. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a second set of bombs hit after the first. The Kremlin did not deny the claims, and its spokesman said such tactics are normal in such situations.
US envoy Steve Witkoff said the US will mediate talks between officials. Moscow has agreed to take part. Mr Zelenskyy said the attack damaged hopes of progress towards peace.
levels.why: It affects hopes of an end to the war and the safety of Ukrainian civilians.

levels.headline: Russian attack kills 33 in Ukraine before peace talks
levels.body:
A Russian attack on an aid centre in Zaporizhzhia in Ukraine has killed 33 people. More than 50 are still missing. Talks between Ukraine and Russia are due in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November, with the United States helping the two sides to talk.
At first the number of dead was lower. Ukrainian officials said the place was a school. The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said that after the first bomb, nine more bombs fell. Russia's government did not deny it. Its spokesman said this kind of attack is normal in such situations.
An American envoy, Steve Witkoff, said the US will help the talks. Mr Zelenskyy said the attack hurt hopes of peace.
levels.why: It could affect whether the war can end.

levels.headline: A deadly attack in Ukraine ahead of peace talks
levels.body:
A Russian attack in the Ukrainian region of Zaporizhzhia has killed 33 people. Over 50 more are still missing. The place that was hit was a centre giving out help to people. Ukrainian officials said it was a school.
The attack came just before talks. Ukraine and Russia are due to meet in a city called Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November. America will help them to talk. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the attack hurt hopes of peace. He said bombs hit twice.
Russia's government did not deny it. A spokesman said this kind of attack is normal in such situations. Russia also sent hundreds of drones at Ukraine on 3 November.
levels.why: People hope the talks will end the war.

levels.headline: Many people killed in Ukraine just before peace talks
levels.body:
Russia and Ukraine have been at war for a long time. Last week, a Russian attack on a place in Ukraine that was giving out help killed 33 people. More than 50 people are missing. Some officials said the place was a school.
A few days later, the two countries are due to talk in a city called Abu Dhabi. America is helping them to talk. They will meet on 10 and 11 November. The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said the attack hurt hopes of peace.
Russia has not said the attack did not happen. A spokesman said this kind of thing is normal in war.
levels.why: People want the war to end and the talks might help.

levels.headline: Lots of people hurt in Ukraine before peace talks
levels.body:
Russia and Ukraine are at war. Last week, Russia attacked a place in Ukraine where people got help. Thirty-three people died. More than fifty are missing. This is very sad.
Soon, the two countries will talk in a city called Abu Dhabi. They will meet on 10 and 11 November. America will help them to talk. The Ukrainian leader said the attack made it harder to hope for peace.
Russia did not say the attack was wrong. Many people hope the talks will help to end the war.
levels.why: People want the war to end.

levels.headline: Sad news before an important talk
levels.body:
There is a war between two countries called Russia and Ukraine. Last week, an attack in Ukraine killed 33 people. It was at a place where people got help. Many more people are still missing. This is very sad.
Soon the two countries will talk. They will meet in a city far away called Abu Dhabi. A friend country, America, will help them to talk. They hope to find a way to stop the war.
The Ukrainian leader said the attack made peace harder. Many people hope the talks will still help.
levels.why: People hope the talks help end the fighting.

levels.headline: Two sides try to stop a very long fight
levels.body:
Imagine two children who have been fighting for a very long time. A friend wants them to stop. The friend asks them to sit down and talk. That is what is happening with Russia and Ukraine.
Last week, there was a very sad attack in Ukraine. Thirty-three people died. It happened at a place where people got help. Soon, the two sides will meet to talk. A friend country, America, will help.
Everyone hopes the talks will help the fighting to stop.
levels.why: Many people hope the fighting ends.

levels.headline: A sad event before a talk
levels.body:
Imagine two children have been in a big argument for years. The head teacher says they must sit and talk. But just before they talk, one of them does something very unkind to the other.
That is a bit like what happened with Russia and Ukraine. They are in a war. Last week, an attack in Ukraine hurt many people. It was at a place where people got help.
Soon they will meet to talk. A friend country will help them. Many people hope it will be a step towards peace.
levels.why: Many people hope the fighting ends soon.

headline: Eurozone inflation rises to 4% in October, highest in three years, as rate rise looms

terms.meaning: Inflation excluding volatile items such as energy, food, alcohol and tobacco.
The ECB's main interest rate, paid on money banks leave with it.
The 20 or so EU countries that use the euro.

levels.headline: Eurozone inflation rises to 4% in October, highest in three years, as rate rise looms
levels.body:
Eurozone inflation rose to 4% in October from 3.8% in September, according to the flash estimate, the highest since September 2023, when it stood at 4.3%. Energy was the main driver, with energy prices 20.8% higher than a year earlier.
Core inflation, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, held steady at 2.5%, while services inflation edged up to 3.3%. Italy saw the biggest jump, to 5.6%, and Lithuania had the highest rate at 6.1%. Germany was an exception: inflation fell to 2.8%, mainly because of a fuel tax cut that took effect on 1 October.
The European Central Bank kept its deposit facility rate at 2.5% on 29 October, after raising it in June and September. Prediction markets put the chance of a quarter-point rise at its 16 to 17 December meeting at about 84%, as reported by Euronews.
levels.why: Rising prices squeeze household budgets across Europe and push the central bank towards higher interest rates.

levels.headline: Euro zone inflation reaches 4%, a three-year high, driven by energy costs
levels.body:
Prices across the euro zone rose 4% in the year to October, up from 3.8% in September, a first estimate showed. It is the highest rate since September 2023. Energy prices were 20.8% higher than a year ago.
Underlying inflation, which leaves out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, was unchanged at 2.5%, and services inflation rose to 3.3%. Italy rose to 5.6% and Lithuania reached 6.1%, the highest. Germany's rate fell to 2.8% thanks to a fuel tax cut from 1 October.
The European Central Bank held its key rate at 2.5% on 29 October after increases in June and September. Markets give about an 84% chance of a quarter-point rise at the 16 to 17 December meeting, according to Euronews.
levels.why: Higher energy prices are feeding through to consumers and raising borrowing costs.

levels.headline: Inflation across the euro area climbs to 4%, its highest in three years
levels.body:
Prices in the countries that use the euro rose 4% in the year to October. In September it was 3.8%. This is the highest rate since September 2023. The main cause was energy, which cost 20.8% more than a year ago.
If you leave out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, prices rose 2.5%, the same as before. Services, such as haircuts and restaurant meals, rose 3.3%. Italy's rate jumped to 5.6% and Lithuania's was the highest at 6.1%. Germany's fell to 2.8% because it cut a fuel tax on 1 October.
The European Central Bank kept its main interest rate at 2.5% on 29 October. It raised it in June and September. Many investors expect a quarter-point rise at its next meeting, on 16 and 17 December.
levels.why: People in Europe are paying more for energy and everyday goods.

levels.headline: Euro area inflation reaches 4%, the highest in three years
levels.body:
Prices in the 20 or so countries that use the euro went up 4% in the year to October. That is the highest since September 2023. In September, it was 3.8%. Energy was the main reason, costing 20.8% more than a year before.
Without energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, prices went up 2.5%, unchanged. Services went up 3.3%. Prices rose fastest in Lithuania, at 6.1%, and Italy, at 5.6%. In Germany inflation fell to 2.8%, partly because fuel tax was cut on 1 October.
The European Central Bank, which sets interest rates for the euro, held its rate at 2.5% on 29 October. It had raised it twice, in June and September. Investors think another rise is likely in December.
levels.why: Higher prices make life more expensive, and higher interest rates make loans cost more.

levels.headline: Prices in Europe are rising faster, at 4% a year
levels.body:
Prices in the countries that use the euro are rising faster. In the year to October, they went up 4%. In September, it was 3.8%. This is the fastest rise for three years. The main reason is that energy costs a lot more than it did a year ago, about a fifth more.
Not everything is going up so fast. Without energy, food, drink and tobacco, prices rose 2.5%. Prices rose most in Lithuania, at 6.1%, and in Italy, at 5.6%. In Germany, they rose less, at 2.8%, because the government cut a tax on fuel.
The bank that sets interest rates for the euro, the European Central Bank, kept its rate at 2.5% on 29 October. Many people think it will raise it in December.
levels.why: It makes shopping and heating dearer, and could make loans cost more.

levels.headline: Prices in Europe go up faster
levels.body:
In Europe, the countries that use the euro have seen prices rise faster. In the year to October, prices went up by 4%. This means something that cost 100 euros a year ago now costs about 104 euros. It is the fastest rise in three years.
Energy is the main cause. It costs about a fifth more than last year. Some countries have had it worse. Lithuania's prices went up 6.1%, and Italy's went up 5.6%. Germany did better, at 2.8%, because it cut a tax on fuel.
The bank that sets interest rates for the euro, the European Central Bank, kept its rate at 2.5%. It might raise it in December to slow the rise in prices.
levels.why: Higher prices make life more expensive for families.

levels.headline: Things in Europe cost more than last year
levels.body:
In Europe, many countries use the euro as their money. Prices there have been going up fast. Something that cost 100 euros last year now costs about 104. This is called inflation. It is the highest for three years.
Energy is the main reason. Things like petrol and heating cost about a fifth more than last year. Some countries have had it worse than others. Prices rose fastest in Lithuania and Italy.
The bank that looks after the euro, the European Central Bank, may raise interest rates in December. This is to slow the price rises down.
levels.why: Things cost more for families, who may have to spend less.

levels.headline: Shops and bills cost more in Europe
levels.body:
Many countries in Europe use the euro as their money. Prices there are going up. Something that cost 100 euros last year now costs about 104. This is called inflation. It is the highest for three years.
Heating and petrol are the main reasons. They cost about a fifth more than last year. People have less money left to spend on other things.
The bank that looks after the euro may raise interest rates in December. This makes borrowing cost more, to try to slow the price rises.
levels.why: Families have to spend more on the same things.

levels.headline: Why sweets cost more than they used to
levels.body:
Imagine your favourite sweet cost 100 pence last year. This year it costs 104 pence. It is only a little more. But if lots of things cost a bit more, it adds up. That is called inflation.
In Europe, many countries use the euro. Prices there have been going up. Heating and petrol cost much more than last year. That makes other things cost more too.
The bank that looks after the euro may make borrowing dearer in December. This is to slow the price rises.
levels.why: It means pocket money buys a little less.

levels.headline: Prices going up a little at a time
levels.body:
Imagine a sweet shop. Last year, a bag of sweets cost 100 pence. This year it costs 104 pence. That is only a little more. But if lots of things cost a bit more, it can add up. That is called inflation.
In some countries in Europe, prices have gone up this year. Heating and petrol cost a lot more. This makes other things cost more too, because it costs more to make and move them.
The grown-ups at the big bank might make borrowing cost more soon. They hope it will stop prices going up so fast.
levels.why: It means money buys a little less than before.
